analysis.one_liner: Bans arsenic-treated wood for playgrounds, decks, and fences and sets safer disposal rules.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, never received a hearing or a vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: Chromated copper arsenic (CCA) is a pesticide infused into pressure-treated lumber to prevent rot, and small amounts of arsenic can leach out of the finished wood onto skin and into soil. This bill would have ordered the EPA to stop the production of CCA-treated wood for residential and child-related uses — playground equipment, decks, fences, walkways, docks — within 60 to 90 days, banned its use in mulch, compost, and soil amendments, and required discarded CCA wood to be buried in lined landfills with groundwater monitoring. It also would have funded a program to teach consumers and schools how to test for arsenic and remove or seal existing treated playground equipment. The bill was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee on the day it was introduced and no further action was ever taken.
analysis.who_benefits: Families with children, homeowners with decks and fences, and school systems gain the most: the ban would stop arsenic from leaching out of new playground equipment and residential structures, keep arsenic-treated ground wood out of mulch and gardens, require safer landfill disposal of discarded treated wood, and provide grants and guidance for testing and removing existing treated equipment at schools. Buyers of substitute-treated lumber would face some near-term price increases.

how_it_helps.text: It would have ended the manufacture of CCA-treated wood for playground equipment, fences, walkways, docks, decks, and other residential and occupational uses within about 90 days, cutting off a route by which arsenic leaches from wood into soil and onto children's hands.
It would have banned arsenic-treated wood from being sold as mulch, compost, or soil amendment, closing a path by which arsenic-treated ground-up wood could end up in home gardens.
It would have required discarded CCA wood to go to lined landfills with leachate collection and groundwater monitoring, reducing the chance that arsenic contaminates drinking water.

It would have created an EPA education program on testing arsenic levels and safely removing or decontaminating existing treated wood, plus grants and technical help for schools to remove or seal treated playground equipment.

analysis.who_pays: Wood preservative chemical manufacturers and treated-wood producers bear the main cost, losing their residential CCA market within months and absorbing retooling expenses. Consumers would likely pay more for pressure-treated lumber made with alternative preservatives, and waste haulers and demolition firms would face higher disposal costs under the hazardous-waste rules.
analysis.who_pays_short: Wood preservative makers and lumber buyers

drawbacks.text: The bill required CCA-treated wood production to stop within 60 days of enactment, an abrupt cutoff that would leave manufacturers, lumberyards, and builders little time to switch to substitute preservatives and could raise prices for decks, fences, and other treated-wood products.

Banning the cheapest widely available wood preservative could raise the cost of pressure-treated lumber for homeowners, contractors, and low-income households building or repairing outdoor structures.

Large amounts of CCA-treated wood were already installed in playgrounds, decks, and fences nationwide; the bill addressed existing wood mainly through testing guidance and limited school grants, so most exposure to already-built structures would have persisted, and reclassifying discarded wood as hazardous waste would have raised disposal costs for demolition and waste-handling firms.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits — faster removal of an arsenic pesticide from children's play structures and safer disposal of discarded treated wood — were real and were later achieved anyway through the EPA's voluntary phase-out, though without the bill's testing guidance, school grants, or lined-landfill disposal rules. The costs were higher prices for treated lumber and an abrupt 60-day production shutdown that could have disrupted supply for decks, fences, and docks. The abruptness was a fair criticism, but for a pesticide whose active ingredient is arsenic, a quick end to residential production is hard to call disproportionate. The main weakness of the outcome is not the bill's design but that it never got a hearing, so the merits were never weighed in public.

outcome.mechanism: The bill went to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 10, 2003 and read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works the same day.
No further action was ever recorded — no hearing, no markup, no committee report, and no Senate vote — through the end of the 108th Congress on January 3, 2005.
It attracted only two cosponsors, both Democrats, during its two-year run.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wood preservative manufacturers and treated-wood producers avoided a mandatory 60-day production shutdown and the bill's disposal requirements; they were also already shifting to substitutes under a separate voluntary EPA phase-out, so they gained time while homeowners got no new testing guidance or school-removal help.

for.name: Bill Nelson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on February 10, 2003 and delivered introductory remarks on it in the Senate.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred to consider the bill after introduction and never held a hearing, markup, or vote on it during the two-year life of the Congress.

against.name: James Inhofe
against.role: Chair, Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, took no recorded action to schedule the bill for consideration at any point in the 108th Congress.

against.name: Wood preservative manufacturers
against.what_they_did: Produced and sold CCA-treated wood for residential use and, in a 2002 agreement with the EPA, agreed to voluntarily stop treating consumer lumber with arsenic by the end of 2003, which took some urgency away from a legislated ban without subjecting the industry to the bill's disposal requirements or school-remediation duties.

sides.party_line_note: Only three Democrats ever put their names on the bill — the sponsor and two Democratic cosponsors — and no Republican supported or opposed it on the record, because the bill never advanced far enough for a vote or a recorded position.

industries.note: The bill would have forced production of chromated copper arsenic preservatives for residential wood to stop within 60 days, cutting off their main consumer market; only railroad ties, marine pilings, and utility poles could continue if EPA deemed those uses safe. For ordinary people this industry's loss was the point — arsenic would stop being infused into backyard and playground wood.

Makers and sellers of pressure-treated lumber would have had to retool around substitute preservatives, with short-term cost and supply disruption, and consumers would likely pay more for treated wood in the near term. Over the longer run the market for treated lumber itself would survive on alternatives.

Reclassifying discarded CCA wood as hazardous waste and requiring lined landfills with leachate and groundwater monitoring would have raised disposal costs but also created demand for higher-spec disposal services. Stricter handling would reduce arsenic reaching groundwater near ordinary landfills.

industries.industry: CCA-treated wood users in Mulch and compost
industries.note: Producers of mulch, compost, and soil amendments would have been barred from using arsenic-treated ground-up wood, removing a cheap feedstock. That cheapness came from material that could put arsenic into home gardens and schoolyards.
